title: Urbanisation & Sustainable Cities
description: Why the world's people are crowding into cities, the problems rapid urban growth creates, and how cities are being redesigned to be sustainable places to live.

notes.heading: 📌 What is Urbanisation? Trends and Megacities
notes.body: Urbanisation is the increasing percentage of a country's population living in towns and cities. It is one of the great transformations of human history: in 1800 only about 3% of people lived in cities; by 2008, for the first time, more than half of humanity was urban; today the figure is approaching 60% and rising. The fastest urbanisation is now happening in Africa and Asia, where cities gain millions of residents every decade. A megacity is a city with more than 10 million inhabitants — Tokyo (around 37 million in its greater area), Delhi, Shanghai, Dhaka and Lagos are among the largest. In 1950 there were only two megacities (New York and Tokyo); today there are more than 30. A primate city dominates its country, being far larger than any other city — Bangkok, for example, dwarfs every other Thai city. Rich countries urbanised first and fastest during the Industrial Revolution; most are now 70-90% urban, while the poorest countries are still urbanising rapidly.

notes.heading: 🔑 Why Cities Grow
notes.body: City populations grow through two processes working together. The first is rural-urban migration — people moving from the countryside to the city. Push factors drive them out of rural areas: farm mechanisation reducing jobs, droughts and poor harvests, low wages, land shortages and few services such as schools and clinics. Pull factors draw them in: the hope of jobs and higher wages, better education for children, hospitals, electricity and running water, and the excitement of city life. Even low-paid informal work (street vending, cleaning, construction) can pay better than subsistence farming. The second process is natural increase — when births exceed deaths within the city itself. Urban populations are young (migrants are mostly young adults of child-bearing age), and cities have better healthcare, so birth rates are relatively high while death rates fall. In most rapidly growing cities, natural increase now adds as many people as migration does. Together these two engines can double a city's population in twenty years — far faster than housing and services can keep up.

notes.heading: 📎 Urban Problems: Housing and Informal Settlements
notes.body: When a city grows faster than its economy and government can cope with, severe problems follow. The most visible is housing: hundreds of thousands of new arrivals cannot afford formal housing, so they build their own — informal settlements (also called slums, shanty towns, favelas in Brazil or barrios elsewhere). These are dense neighbourhoods of self-built shelters made from wood, corrugated iron and scrap, often on land the residents do not own — steep hillsides, floodplains, railway edges or marshes. Informal settlements typically lack secure tenure (the legal right to stay, risking eviction), clean water, sanitation, electricity, rubbish collection and paved roads. Overcrowding and open sewage spread disease; flimsy materials are vulnerable to fire, floods and landslides. Yet these places are also full of energy and enterprise: residents build businesses, organise their own communities and improve their homes over time. More than a billion people — roughly one in eight humans — live in informal settlements today.

notes.heading: 📎 Urban Problems: Congestion, Pollution and Inequality
notes.body: Beyond housing, rapid urban growth strains every system. Congestion: roads built for thousands now carry millions; in cities like Lagos, Dhaka or Jakarta, commuters can spend three or four hours a day in traffic, wasting fuel and working time. Pollution: vehicle exhaust, factory emissions and burning waste create smog that damages lungs — air pollution kills millions of people prematurely each year, most of them in cities; untreated sewage and industrial waste contaminate rivers and groundwater; mountains of uncollected rubbish attract rats and disease. Water and energy: demand outstrips supply, causing rationing and blackouts. Inequality: cities concentrate wealth and poverty side by side — gated communities with swimming pools may sit next to informal settlements without toilets. The wealthy enjoy private healthcare, schools and security while the poor depend on overstretched public services. In some cities this inequality fuels crime and social tension. Rich-world cities face different versions of the same issues: homelessness, unaffordable housing, ageing infrastructure and suburban sprawl eating up countryside.

notes.heading: 💡 Managing Rapid Urban Growth
notes.body: Cities have tried many strategies to manage runaway growth, with mixed success. Slum clearance — demolishing informal settlements — usually fails: it destroys communities and livelihoods, and displaced families simply build new shanties elsewhere. Site-and-service schemes work better: the government provides a legal plot of land with water, sanitation and electricity, and families build their own homes on it over time. Self-help and upgrading (improvement) schemes improve existing settlements in place — paving roads, installing sewers and standpipes, legalising land tenure — recognising that residents themselves are the best builders of their neighbourhoods. Building affordable social housing helps but rarely keeps pace with demand. Improving rural areas — better schools, clinics, irrigation and rural jobs — can slow migration at the source. Some governments build entirely new planned cities or move their capital (as Brazil did with Brasília) to draw growth away from overcrowded centres. The most successful approaches combine several strategies and involve residents in decisions rather than imposing solutions from above.

notes.heading: 📌 What Makes a City Sustainable?
notes.body: A sustainable city meets the needs of its people today without damaging the environment or the ability of future generations to meet their needs — balancing economic opportunity, quality of life and environmental protection. Key features include: Transport — prioritising walking, cycling and fast, affordable public transport (metros, trams, bus rapid transit) over private cars cuts congestion, pollution and carbon emissions. Green space — parks, street trees, green roofs and urban farms cool the city, absorb floodwater, support wildlife and improve mental and physical health. Energy — efficient buildings, solar panels and renewable power reduce the city's carbon footprint; districts can capture waste heat or burn rubbish to generate electricity. Waste — reducing, reusing and recycling (a circular economy approach) keeps resources in use and landfill small. Water — harvesting rainwater, recycling greywater and protecting wetlands guards against both drought and flooding. Fairness — sustainability is social as well as environmental: affordable housing and services must be within everyone's reach. Compact, mixed-use design — homes, jobs and shops close together — cuts the need to travel at all.

notes.heading: 💡 Sustainable Cities in Action
notes.body: No city is perfectly sustainable, but many lead the way. Curitiba, Brazil, became famous for its Bus Rapid Transit system — dedicated bus lanes with prepaid boarding tubes carrying millions of passengers daily at a fraction of the cost of a metro — alongside parks built on floodplains (cheaper than flood defences) and a recycling programme where poor residents exchange rubbish for food. Copenhagen, Denmark, invests so heavily in cycling that bicycles outnumber cars in the city centre, and it aims to be carbon neutral — districts are heated efficiently and much power comes from wind. Singapore manages land, water and greenery together: a garden city with tree-lined roads, rooftop gardens, world-class water recycling (NEWater) and excellent public transport. Freiburg, Germany, built the eco-district of Vauban with solar homes that generate more energy than they use and streets designed for trams and children rather than cars. Masdar City in the UAE is an experimental low-carbon city in the desert. The lesson from all of them: sustainable design usually saves money in the long run and makes cities healthier and happier — but it requires long-term planning and political will.

flashcards.definition: The increasing percentage of a country's population living in towns and cities.
flashcards.example: China urbanised from under 20% urban in 1980 to over 60% today — one of the fastest shifts in history.

flashcards.definition: A city with a population of more than 10 million people.
flashcards.example: Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, Dhaka and Lagos are all megacities; Tokyo's greater area holds around 37 million people.

flashcards.definition: The movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities, usually in search of work and better services.
flashcards.example: A farming family leaving a drought-hit village to find factory work in Lagos is rural-urban migration.

flashcards.definition: Population growth within a place that occurs when the birth rate exceeds the death rate.
flashcards.example: Young city populations with good healthcare have high birth rates and falling death rates, adding as many people as migration does.

flashcards.definition: A neighbourhood of self-built housing on land residents often do not legally own, usually lacking basic services like water, sanitation and electricity.
flashcards.example: Brazil's favelas and India's bustees are informal settlements housing more than a billion people worldwide.

flashcards.definition: The legal right to remain in your home without the risk of eviction.
flashcards.example: Granting secure tenure lets informal-settlement families invest in improving their homes without fear of demolition.

flashcards.definition: Overcrowding of roads by traffic, causing slow journeys, wasted time and fuel, and air pollution.
flashcards.example: In Jakarta and Lagos, commuters can spend three to four hours a day stuck in traffic.

flashcards.definition: A housing strategy where government provides a legal plot with basic services (water, sanitation, electricity) and families build their own homes on it.
flashcards.example: Families receive a serviced plot and gradually construct and improve their house as they can afford to.

flashcards.definition: Improving existing informal settlements in place — paving roads, installing sewers and legalising tenure — rather than demolishing them.
flashcards.example: Connecting a favela to mains water and giving residents land rights improves lives without destroying the community.

flashcards.definition: A city designed to meet people's needs today while protecting the environment and resources for future generations.
flashcards.example: A sustainable city combines public transport, green space, renewable energy and recycling with affordable housing for all.

flashcards.definition: A high-capacity bus system with dedicated lanes and prepaid stations, giving metro-like service at much lower cost.
flashcards.example: Curitiba's BRT carries millions of passengers a day and has been copied by cities across the world.

flashcards.definition: Balancing the carbon dioxide released with an equal amount removed or avoided, giving net zero emissions.
flashcards.example: Copenhagen aims to be carbon neutral through wind power, district heating and cycling.

choices: The movement of people from cities to the countryside
The increasing percentage of a population living in towns and cities
The building of roads between cities
The growth of farming around cities
questions.explanation: Urbanisation is measured as the rising share of a country's people living in urban areas — driven by rural-urban migration and natural increase in cities.

choices: A city with more than 1 million people
A city with more than 10 million people
The capital city of any country
Any city with a skyscraper
questions.explanation: A megacity has over 10 million inhabitants. Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, Dhaka and Lagos all qualify; in 1950 there were only two in the world.

questions.stem: Which two processes together make city populations grow?
choices: Rural-urban migration and natural increase
Trade and tourism
Counter-urbanisation and suburbanisation
Industrialisation and deindustrialisation
questions.explanation: Cities grow because migrants arrive from the countryside and because births exceed deaths within the city itself. In most fast-growing cities, natural increase now contributes as much as migration.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a pull factor attracting people to cities?
choices: Farm machinery reducing rural jobs
Drought and poor harvests
Better-paid jobs, schools and hospitals in the city
Land shortages in the countryside
questions.explanation: Jobs, education, healthcare and utilities are urban attractions — pull factors. Mechanisation, drought and land shortage are push factors that drive people out of rural areas.

questions.stem: Why do fast-growing cities have high rates of natural increase?
choices: City populations are mostly elderly
Migrants are mostly young adults, and better urban healthcare means more births and fewer deaths
Governments pay city dwellers to have children
Cities have unlimited food supplies
questions.explanation: Rural-urban migrants are typically young adults of child-bearing age. Combined with better hospitals and sanitation lowering death rates, this produces rapid natural increase within the city.

choices: A wealthy gated community
A government-built housing estate
A neighbourhood of self-built housing, usually on land residents do not legally own, lacking services like water and sanitation
A temporary campsite for tourists
questions.explanation: Informal settlements (slums, favelas, shanty towns) are built by residents themselves, often without secure tenure, piped water, sewers or electricity — and house more than a billion people worldwide.

questions.stem: Why do informal settlements often develop on steep hillsides or floodplains?
choices: These locations have the best views
The land is usually unsafe or undesirable, so nobody stops poor migrants settling there
The government always gives this land to new arrivals
These areas have the best soil for farming in the city
questions.explanation: New migrants cannot afford safe, legal land, so they occupy marginal sites others avoid — but that leaves them exposed to landslides, flooding and eviction.

questions.stem: A city demolishes a large informal settlement and relocates residents to a site 40 km away. Why does this strategy usually fail?
choices: It destroys communities and livelihoods, and displaced families often build new informal settlements elsewhere
The new housing is always too comfortable
Residents prefer to live abroad afterwards
Demolition is too cheap to be effective
questions.explanation: Slum clearance breaks up social networks and moves people far from their jobs; unable to afford alternatives, families typically form new shanties closer to work. Upgrading in place works far better.

choices: The government provides a legal plot with water, sanitation and electricity, and families build their own homes on it
A scheme that clears all informal settlements
A tax on new housing developments
A free bus service for city workers
questions.explanation: Site-and-service schemes supply the expensive parts poor families cannot manage alone — legal land and infrastructure — while letting residents build housing themselves over time, which they do well and cheaply.

questions.stem: Which feature is central to a sustainable city?
choices: Prioritising private car use with more motorways
Fast, affordable public transport combined with walking and cycling
Removing all green space to build more housing
Sending all waste to landfill
questions.explanation: Sustainable transport puts walking, cycling and public transit ahead of private cars — cutting congestion, air pollution and carbon emissions while making the city healthier and fairer.

questions.stem: How does green space help make a city more sustainable?
choices: It only makes the city look nicer
Parks and trees cool the city, absorb floodwater, support wildlife and improve residents' health
It increases land prices so more tax is collected
It provides space for more car parks
questions.explanation: Green space delivers multiple benefits at once: shade and cooling in heatwaves, flood absorption, habitats for wildlife, cleaner air and better mental and physical health for residents.

questions.stem: Curitiba in Brazil is world-famous for which sustainable transport innovation?
choices: The world's first underground metro
Bus Rapid Transit — dedicated bus lanes with prepaid boarding stations giving metro-like service cheaply
Banning all public transport in favour of cars
A city-wide monorail
questions.explanation: Curitiba's BRT carries millions of passengers daily at a fraction of a metro's cost, proving that clever bus design can move a city sustainably — the model has been copied worldwide.

questions.stem: Curitiba built many of its parks on floodplains instead of building expensive concrete flood defences. Why is this an example of sustainable planning?
choices: It achieves flood protection and public green space at the same time, at lower cost
It prevents anyone from using the land at all
It increases flooding so more rain is collected
Parks always make flooding worse
questions.explanation: This is joined-up thinking: letting floodplains flood naturally into parks stores water safely, saves money on defences and creates recreation space — one solution serving several needs, the hallmark of sustainability.

questions.stem: Copenhagen aims to be carbon neutral. Which combination of policies best supports this goal?
choices: More motorways and free parking
Wind power, efficient district heating and heavy investment in cycling
Coal power stations inside the city
Encouraging longer car commutes from the suburbs
questions.explanation: Cutting carbon requires cleaner energy supply (wind, district heating) and lower demand — Copenhagen's cycling culture means bikes outnumber cars in the centre, eliminating thousands of car journeys daily.

questions.stem: A city wants to reduce car use. Which plan would a geographer judge most sustainable overall?
choices: Building a wider ring road so cars can drive faster
Building compact, mixed-use neighbourhoods where homes, jobs and shops are close together, served by trams and cycle lanes
Giving every household a subsidy to buy a second car
Moving all shops to out-of-town retail parks
questions.explanation: Mixed-use, compact design removes the need to travel far in the first place, while trams and cycle lanes handle the journeys that remain. Bigger roads typically fill with new traffic (induced demand) and out-of-town retail increases car dependence.
